A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Token Sample Complexity of Attention by the same authors. Their main text, equations, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v2 reports original Monte Carlo experiments on Gaussian tokens and attention-output convergence experiments using BigBird on Wikipedia and CC-News, including appendix results.

after.justification: v3 retains original convergence experiments and adds uniform-sphere simulations, BERT experiments, structured-sampling tests, and downstream classification results.

M1.justification: The underlying single-head and multi-head attention operators remain unchanged. Absorbing the attention scaling into the query/key matrices clarifies notation. The new architectures and sampling patterns are experimental settings, while the revised horizon changes the analysis rather than the proposed computational method.

E1.justification: v3 adds an 11-category arxiv-classification task and synthetic tokens uniformly distributed on a unit sphere in dimension 50. These substantially extend coverage beyond v2's Gaussian simulations and Wikipedia/CC-News attention-statistics experiments, which are retained.

E2.justification: Population or full-context attention remains the reference for finite-token approximation, with this comparison extended to classification. BERT supplies an additional validation architecture, and window/hybrid sampling supplies robustness conditions; no competing baseline algorithm is introduced or removed.

E3.justification: v3 adds BERT evaluation, local-window sampling with 50 random keys, and half-local/half-random sampling. Classification introduces three-epoch fine-tuning, 2400 test documents, 64–4096 sampled keys, and prediction-level metrics. Horizon diagnostics use the revised definition. The original reference-token and subsample-size settings remain in Appendix A.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether slowdown persists beyond Gaussian tokens, BigBird's sparse architecture, and i.i.d. key sampling (Figures 8–11). Figure 2 additionally stratifies downstream behavior by horizon. These directly investigate robustness and applicability questions that v2's experiments did not establish.

E5.justification: v3 reports five Monte Carlo repetitions and ±3σ bands for classification, and 500–1000 subsamples with ±3 standard-error bands for BERT. The original 500-repetition budget is retained. Some uncertainty labeling is removed: v2 Figure 5 explicitly identifies 95% confidence intervals, whereas corresponding v3 Figure 7 does not.

E6.justification: New classification results report 86.4% dense accuracy and 84.5% at 1101 sampled keys, alongside new BERT, sphere, and windowed-sampling results. Existing BigBird plots also change: the mean horizon-rate correlation becomes -0.64 from -0.68 under the revised horizon definition. Figure 6's exact exponents are inconsistent between legend and caption, although both report sub-parametric convergence.

T1.justification: v3 replaces Ψ = ||Σ||₂||Σ^(1/2)A||₂² with H² = ||Σ^(1/2)AΣ^(1/2)||₂² in the moment-rate bounds, supported by ellipsoidal truncation and optimization over an invertible matrix. It adds general-set convergence, MSE and layer-composition corollaries, a heavy-tail counterexample argument, and polynomial-radius bounds under additional assumptions in Appendix E. The uniform-denominator proof is substantially revised, but its new sample-size threshold is not reconciled with Theorem 4.2.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion extend the central contribution from attention-map and moment convergence to horizon-dependent recovery of full-network logits, predictions, and classification accuracy. The refined geometric horizon also becomes a more explicit organizing claim.

C2.justification: v3 explains slowdown through alignment between attention directions and high-variance token directions. It corrects the earlier suggestion that the original text experiments tested non-i.i.d. sampling, distinguishing dependent source text from structured subsampling. It also adds heavy-tail failure discussion and interprets downstream results as diminishing returns from additional keys.

D1.justification: v3 replaces the supplementary-code statement with an explicit repository link and supplies details for the new experiments, including mean pooling, fine-tuning duration, and window/hybrid construction. The existing BigBird reference-token, subsample-size, and repetition details are relocated to Appendix A rather than removed.

R1.justification: The reference list is unchanged. Section 2 removes the distinction that this work studies moments whereas Boursier and Boyer study L2 error, consistent with v3's added MSE result. Other research positioning remains substantially stable.

P1.justification: The main section sequence remains intact. v3 tightens explanatory passages and proof sketches, moves experimental appendix material ahead of the theoretical tools, and relocates implementation details. Affiliations, correspondence information, publication text, and acknowledgements are also updated.

P2.justification: v3 adds substantial multipanel classification, BERT, and structured-sampling figures. Existing horizon plots are redrawn with revised axes and legends, and BigBird covariance displays are combined with BERT panels in Figure 9. The expanded experimental figures move from the final appendix to Appendix A.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens practical validation: v2 measured attention moments, while v3 directly tests downstream predictions and accuracy and checks architectural and sampling robustness. The geometric refinement and clearer treatment of the i.i.d. assumption also improve explanatory value. These gains outweigh remaining inconsistencies, including Figure 6's conflicting exponents and the unreconciled theorem/proof sample-size thresholds, which limit confidence in precise quantitative claims.
